None of my feedback from https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2806#issuecomment-379988839 has been addressed, either in the issue or in this PR (about naming, need a companion placeholder feature, and interactions with async decoding).

Correction: naming issue was acknowledged [here](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2806#issuecomment-380191071) with an offer to discuss further but no change was made and the discussion never happened. I realize this is a bit bikesheddy, but I still think my proposal is better for clarity and possible future extensibility. 

Further correction: need for a placeholder was also acknowledged with "It makes sense to me to provide a way for developers to specify their own placeholders" but that has not been done in this PR.

Also, the feedback that this should apply to `<picture>` has not been addressed. and @smfr's feedback that it should work with `srcset` in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2806#issuecomment-379996290 (perhaps that is just naturally true but it was not explained).

For avoidance of doubt, we (WebKit) are not enthusiastic about implementing a feature where much of our feedback was not taken into account, although we agree with the general use case.

And finally, the `iframe` aspect of this was discussed in the issue a bit, but we didn't think about it as closely. I am not sure if that has the same tradeoffs and developer demand. I suggest splitting it into a separate PR because we may not be able to figure out quickly if we support that aspect, even if our points of feedback as to `img` were addressed.

@othermaciej: Sorry for the delayed response. Responses to your comments are below. I appreciate your feedback and will be incorporating it into an updated PR. I’m sorry if I gave the impression that I wasn’t taking your feedback into account. > I wish there was a way to make this a boolean instead of a tristate, since boolean attributes have much sweeter syntax in HTML. I tried to address this [here](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2806#issuecomment-380191071), where I mentioned the three cases we are trying to handle well. Would you like to discuss this further? > Bikeshed comment: If it has to be a tristate, maybe we can have more meaningful keywords than `on` and `off`. How about `load=lazy`, `load=eager`, `load=auto`? This also makes it feasible to add other values if a fourth useful state should ever be discovered. And it's also a bit more consistent with the `decoding` attribute (on which see more below). I also mentioned there that `on` and `off` seemed clearer to me, but have since warmed to your alternative. In particular, it would be nice to introduce the term `eager` here because we hope to follow up with feature policy that restricts eager loading. I also like the parallel to `decoding`. My one concern is that we’d be co-opting the term `load` for a single dimension of loading behavior, namely, how lazily we will load. A new feature would have to use some terms other than `load` if it wanted control over another dimension of loading. > Many developer-rolled versions of lazy loading use some form of placeholder so that seems like an essential feature. CSS `background-image` with a `data:` URL seems like a pretty inelegant (and potentially inefficient) way to do it I still think a developer-provided placeholder is largely orthogonal to lazyloading. The platform should have a more elegant way to show a placeholder while something loads, independent of whether native lazyloading is supported. I’d prefer for someone other than me to champion such a feature and not to couple it with lazyloading. Does that work for you? > It would be good to figure out how this interacts with [async decoding](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/1920). Should lazy-loaded images be be asynchronously decoded as if `decoding=async` was specified? I think probably yes, as the use cases for sync decoding don't seem to be consistent with lazy loading. At the extreme you could think of `lazy` as an additional decoding state, though that might be stretching the attribute too far. I tried to address this as well in my previous response where I said the lazyload attribute is different from (and orthogonal to) images with `decoding=async`. Lazyload means defer loading until needed, whereas `decoding=async` means do not block presentation. I can see wanting to make decoding async for some lazyloaded images, but I could also see wanting to decode an image as fast as possible (i.e., sync) if the user scrolled quickly to it. Does this orthogonality make sense to you? I think we could tie the features together in the future without breaking content if you thought that doing so was important, but for now we could proceed with them as not affecting each other. > Also, the feedback that this should apply to `` has not been addressed. and @smfr's feedback that it should work with `srcset` in [#2806 (comment)](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2806#issuecomment-379996290) (perhaps that is just naturally true but it was not explained). Sorry that I didn't address this point earlier. I agree that this should apply to ``, even though the current spec patch does not do so. (I.e., `` will not lazyload.) Do you think it's OK to add `lazyload=""` (or `load=""`) to `` in a second, follow-on PR? Note that the spec as written (as well as Chrome's implementation) will lazyload an ``. > And finally, the `iframe` aspect of this was discussed in the issue a bit, but we didn't think about it as closely. I am not sure if that has the same tradeoffs and developer demand. I suggest splitting it into a separate PR because we may not be able to figure out quickly if we support that aspect, even if our points of feedback as to `img` were addressed. I’d prefer we discuss the feature holistically; I hope our discussion on iframe will be fruitful and iterate with lower latency.

> @othermaciej: Sorry for the delayed response. Responses to your comments are below. I appreciate your feedback and will be incorporating it into an updated PR. I’m sorry if I gave the impression that I wasn’t taking your feedback into account. I appreciate the response. I think there may be a general problem with feedback sometimes being dropped when the discussion venue changes (from issue to PR, from one PR to another PR, etc). Not sure how to overcome that. > My one concern is that we’d be co-opting the term `load` for a single dimension of loading behavior, namely, how lazily we will load. A new feature would have to use some terms other than `load` if it wanted control over another dimension of loading. One way to be super forward looking to this possibility is to make the attribute take a token list, even though currently it would only be able to hold exactly one token. This would guarantee ability to add tokens without breaking parsing of existing values. A simpler way to be forward compatible in this way is to require stripping everything in the attribute value following a space before checking for valid values. Not sure either of these forward-compatibility measures is worth it. > I still think a developer-provided placeholder is largely orthogonal to lazyloading. What do you intend to show as a placeholder if lazy loading can't keep up? I'm concerned that there might not be any acceptable alternative that can be provided completely by the browser. That's what makes me think it is not completely orthogonal. But if there is a reasonably acceptable placeholder that the browser can provide, I'd agree. > I can see wanting to make decoding async for some lazyloaded images, but I could also see wanting to decode an image as fast as possible (i.e., sync) if the user scrolled quickly to it. Does this orthogonality make sense to you? sync doesn't necessarily make decoding faster, it just makes it block and thus potentially cause jittery scrolling. I think the combination of `load=lazy decoding=sync` doesn't really make sense. If the browser manages to perform lazy loads fast enough to keep with the user's scrolling, it would cause scrolling jitter. If the user outpaces the browser's loading, then the user sees a placeholder but then the sync decode *still* causes jitter. Doesn't seem like this would ever be right. That said, the default for `decoding` is `auto`, so unless someone says this explicitly, the browser could choose to use async decoding for lazy loaded images. So I agree no change is really needed. You say: > Sorry that I didn't address this point earlier. I agree that this should apply to ``, even though the current spec patch does not do so. (I.e., `` will not lazyload.) Do you think it's OK to add `lazyload=""` (or `load=""`) to `` in a second, follow-on PR? But on the other hand you say: > I’d prefer we discuss the feature holistically; I hope our discussion on iframe will be fruitful and iterate with lower latency. These stances seem somewhat contradictory. Do you want to discuss the feature holistically or not? To be more explicit, I can't see a good rationale for deferring `picture` to a later PR, but still including lazy loading for `iframe`. Surely `picture` is more obviously related to `img`. For example, I expect the related Feature Policy proposals would want to apply to `picture` the sane as `omg` (while, conversely, it may be desirable to have separate policies for images and frames). (Side note: one important question is whether lazy loading should go on `picture` or on `source`.) I think `iframe` raises a bunch of different issues. If the browser tries to load frames ahead of time to keep up with the user's scrolling, it can't just assume that a background load (and possibly async decode) will make it ready to display. It may require loading many resources plus executing script. It seems to me there is high risk this will cause scrolling glitches. (But perhaps Chrome has relevant implementation experience to show it doesn't). That's why I am a bit less convinced in the `iframe` case than the image case. But I'll see if we can provide more detailed feedback. > Note that the spec as written (as well as Chrome's implementation) will lazyload an ``. Thanks for clarifying the srcset point.

@othermaciej > One way to be super forward looking to this possibility is to make the attribute take a token list, even though currently it would only be able to hold exactly one token. This would guarantee ability to add tokens without breaking parsing of existing values. A simpler way to be forward compatible in this way is to require stripping everything in the attribute value following a space before checking for valid values. Not sure either of these forward-compatibility measures is worth it. Yeah, I don’t think either of these forward-compatibility measures is worth it. I’ll update the PR to use `load=auto|eager|lazy`. > What do you intend to show as a placeholder if lazy loading can't keep up? I'm concerned that there might not be any acceptable alternative that can be provided completely by the browser. That's what makes me think it is not completely orthogonal. But if there is a reasonably acceptable placeholder that the browser can provide, I'd agree. The Chrome implementation shows an empty rectangle wherever a not-yet-loaded image should be. We are tuning lazyloading to be conservative so that seeing a not-yet-loaded image in the viewport is about as common as without lazyloading. > That said, the default for `decoding` is `auto`, so unless someone says this explicitly, the browser could choose to use async decoding for lazy loaded images. So I agree no change is really needed. Great. > These stances seem somewhat contradictory. Do you want to discuss the feature holistically or not? Good point. I do want to discuss the feature holistically, so I’ll update the PR to include ``. My first thought is that `load=lazy` should go on `picture` and not `source` because `source` can contain files other than images, e.g., with `

@bengreenstein note that the `source` element already has different authoring and processing requirements depending on its parent. So it should be fine to add this attribute and only have it take effect when the parent element is `picture`.
@annevk that's a great point, and adding to `source` is otherwise semantically simpler than to `picture`.
Thank you all for your work here. I was pleasantly surprised to find this still being actively worked on and I look forward to the day when lazyloading images will be as simple as is specced here.

There seemed to be some consensus on `load=lazy|eager|auto`, so I updated the PR. I haven't added changes for `picture` yet. See a [comment](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2806#issuecomment-470328532) from @addyosmani who had a good point. I'm curious what other people's thoughts are about applying the `load` attribute from an `img` inside a `picture` to `source`.

BTW if the goal is to specify lazy loading in only one place, then a better place is ``, with a rule that nested `` will inherit the behavior. It doesn't have the same problem, because the `` element is always parsed before its children and appears textually before (though I am not sure how it would interact with preload scanning).

From a preload scanner perspective, if we want to ensure loading behavior is parsed as early as possible, I could see this working (any child `` inherits the parent ``s loading preferences). Something like this? ```html
Further thoughts on this. The goal of this change is to comprehensively provide lazy loading. So it's worth considering other embedding elements besides ``, `

@othermaciej > @bengreenstein If we did that, we'd also want to provide an alternate way of setting it, since `` is not required to contain an ``. But I'm also not sure it is a super good idea. Ideally, a `` for a `` should be able to start loading as soon as it's parsed if it is an eager load. This will generally be earlier than the nested `` is parsed. So by the time the browser is told to do lazy loading, it's too late and it may have started the load already. > > In addition, browsers that do preload scanning (i.e. a quick scan to start loading sub resources even before the parser has reached them, such as due to a blocking script) also won't see the `` before the ``. > > For these reasons, I don't think the suggestion will actually work, despite being syntactically neat. Or at least, to make it would would require never starting the load for a `` until the close tag of `` is hit, which would potentially be a performance hit. This is not how `picture` is defined and implemented. The `img` is in fact required. Nothing loads at all if there is no `img`. Even the speculative parser should wait for the `img` before starting a load. The `img` element owns the image loading algorithm. This setup makes me think the `img` and only the `img` should have the `load` attribute. If the image loading algorithm takes `load` into account, then it should just work for `picture` as well.

> This setup makes me think the img and only the img should have the load attribute. If the image loading algorithm takes load into account, then it should just work for picture as well.

Yes, I agree. As a Web author, I would find it confusing if any attributes set on the `picture` element were effectively being automatically set on the child `img` element, when the `picture` element is designed purely to influence the image source.

> `object`: can embed images or frames as well as plugins, so it ought to be added and supported at least in its image and frame states (maybe not plugin). I don't believe this element to be super common but a complete solution ought to cover it.

We have avoided extending `object` with new features since `object` was too overloaded to begin with. For example, `decoding`, `srcset`, `sandbox`, `allow` do not exist on `object`. So we shouldn't add `load` on `object`.

Similarly, `input type=image` lacks new image features. I think this one is basically considered a legacy feature and as far as I can tell there isn't much interest in improving it.

From the [spec](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/embedded-content.html#the-picture-element):

> The `picture` element is a container which provides multiple sources to its contained `img` element

I don't believe the `source` or `picture` elements do any fetching themselves but rather change the `src` of the contained `img`. If this is the case I would say keeping `load=lazy` on the `img`, rather than on the `picture`, is preferable.

EDIT: reference the correct part of the spec
What you quoted is a requirement for authors. But yes, the `img` does the loading.

@zcorpan sorry for the misinformation about `picture`. 

I guess that resolves the issue during regular parsing, with the rule of following the `load` attribute on the contained `img`.

Re preloading: from code inspection, WebKit's preload scanner does not wait until it sees an `img` inside `picture` before preloading a `source`, if it sees one whose conditions from are matched. I expect the one in Blink does the same, unless it has been changed dramatically since the fork. The preload scanner is in general ok with some false positives as long as the rate is low enough. But in the case of lazy loading it would defeat the purpose of the feature. I will ask around whether it would be practical to make the preload scanner always wait for the nested `img`.

The case against supporting semi-obsolete elements seems reasonable. Further question: what would this mean for the planned Feature Policy to flip the default? Would it retain eager image loading for these types of image-bearing elements?

That would leave only the `poster` attribute on `video` to consider.

> I expect the one in Blink does the same, unless it has been changed dramatically since the fork.

@yoavweiss ?

> Further question: what would this mean for the planned Feature Policy to flip the default? Would it retain eager image loading for these types of image-bearing elements?

I think that would fall out from not supporting the lazy load feature, but I don't have a strong opinion.

For `video`, it seems possible to support `load` there also and have it apply to both the poster image and the media resource itself. `load` and `preload` are different axes:

* `preload`: how much should be loaded?
* `load`: when should it be loaded?

The semantics of combining them for the media resource could be something like


`preload`/`load` | `lazy`                               | `auto`                                    | `eager`
-----------------|--------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|---------------
`none`           | Load nothing                         | Load nothing                              | Load nothing
`metadata`       | When visible, load metadata          | UA-defined when to load metadata          | Eagerly load metadata
`auto`           | When visible, load UA-defined amount | UA-defined when to load UA-defined amount | Eagerly load UA-defined amount

For `poster` it would apply like for `img`.

A problem with adding the attribute to `video` however is that name `load` is already taken by the `load()` method. So it needs a different name, at least on media elements, if we want to provide this feature for videos. This article https://developers.google.com/web/fundamentals/performance/lazy-loading-guidance/images-and-video/ and the fact that there exist WordPress plugins and JS libraries for lazy-loading video suggest that there is demand. (YouTube video embeds are probably handled by `iframe`, but still.)
Suggestion for a different name if we need it: `loadpolicy`

Seconding @zcorpan, I would consider `object` obsolete, although not officially so. I think modern sites should be using iframe or img instead. I think it's generally kept in the non-obsolete portions of the spec because the spec still allows plugins. (I.e., it's kept for purposes of Flash.) And for `input type=image`, also semi-obsolete, compared to ``.

I'd like to state my support to everything @zcorpan said. If we set the `load` attribute on HTMLImageElement, `` and `srcset` support should naturally fall off of that, as HTMLImageElement is the one driving image loading. @othermaciej, regarding preloading: > Re preloading: from code inspection, WebKit's preload scanner does not wait until it sees an `img` inside `picture` before preloading a `source`, if it sees one whose conditions from are matched. I expect the one in Blink does the same, unless it has been changed dramatically since the fork. `` is required for picture to actually trigger a load in Blink's [HTMLPreloadScanner](https://cs.chromium.org/chromium/src/third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/parser/html_preload_scanner.cc?sq=package:chromium&dr=CSs&g=0&l=201) (And historically, support in both engines was added independently after the fork) > The preload scanner is in general ok with some false positives as long as the rate is low enough. But in the case of lazy loading it would defeat the purpose of the feature. I will ask around whether it would be practical to make the preload scanner always wait for the nested `img`. I agree that preload scanner support is a requirement here, and otherwise it would defeat the feature's purpose. I'm sure there are more authoritative folks than me on that front, but my understanding is that WebKit's HTMLPreloadScanner's architecture would enable it to implement something very similar to Blink's, or even adapt the current [pictureState](https://github.com/WebKit/webkit/blob/master/Source/WebCore/html/parser/HTMLPreloadScanner.cpp#L128) check and make sure it only calls `setUrlToLoad` when an image tag is encountered inside the picture tag.

Hello everyone, Anwar here, web developper. First of all, I would like to thank you all for the time you put in this feature request. I think this will definitively improve the experience of millions of users, and this will help move towards the progressive web experience we all dream about. I read with attention this feed and I came up with one question: did you considered network failures in the lazy loading algorithm? For example : 1. You are viewing a picture gallery with 5 rows of images. The 2 first rows of images are visible on the viewport after the page loaded, while the 3 remaining rows are hidden below the screen. 2. You scroll and the browser is lazy loading the 3rd row. 3. Then you loose connectivity but keep scrolling up to the 4th row. The browser displays a "broke image icon", because of the network failure, for each images of this row. 4. Your network comes back, and you scroll to the 5th row. The browser manages to lazy load this row. 5. You scroll back to the failing row, the 4th. **What should happen here?** I know that, for example, one of the popular library for lazy loading images, [https://github.com/verlok/lazyload](https://github.com/verlok/lazyload), is not currently supporting network failures (I opened [an issue](https://github.com/verlok/lazyload/issues/324) about it by the way, might be interesting to see the author point of view about this issue). You can try the same behavior on this link : [https://www.andreaverlicchi.eu/lazyload/demos/image_simple.html](https://www.andreaverlicchi.eu/lazyload/demos/image_simple.html). In one hand, if we consider network state not being in the scope of this feature, this would let us, the web developper, handle this exception by building a specific lazy loading algorithm to handle such a case (because we would have to register to the IntersectionObserver API callback to try to load the image again), which for me would be a loss since I am duplicating the (future) native lazy loading browser behavior. In another hand, we could agree on the fact that network fluctuations is a specific case to address and must not be included in the algorithm but handled by the user because this should be up to the developper to decide whether this can affect the user experience or not (depending the nature of the web app). If this is something we could opt-in to the user, and only if such a behavior is easy to handle and predictable regarding the browser capability to listen to the network state change (knowing that `window.addEvenListener('offline')` is in living standard now, we might safely say this should be feasable), I came up with a 4th option for the `load` attribute: `load=lazy-revive | lazy | eager | auto`. What you guys think? I must admit I rapidly browsed the spec, so if I am missing something do not hesitate to point it out. I hope my input will help you drive this conversation to a point where we all agree on the direction this promissing feature should orientate. **Edit** The author of lazyload, verlok, came back to me. > I think you can already do something like that. > > When the connection comes back: > > - select all the images with the error class set > - cycle them and remove their data-processed attribute and the error class > - call .update() on the LazyLoad instance > > This will make LazyLoad re-consider all the images should do already. So it seems it is clearly opt-in to the user. I guess if we go on this path, we could imagine managing which medias should be lazy loading using a Javascript API, like we can control when a video can be paused/resumed with `.play()`. What came up on my mind is a method that we could call to tell the browser we want to specifically register an image for being processed by the algorithm, like : ```html ``` ```javascript window.addEventListener('online', () => { const failedImages = document.querySelectorAll('img[data-failed],picture[data-failed]'); for (const image of failedImages) { image.removeAttribute('data-failed'); image.load(); } }); ``` Where `image.load()` is triggering the load algorithm (lazy or not). One of the caveat with this code is that if the network went offline again in the same time on the loop, the image will never be loaded again (unless there is a Javascript method to know if an image has failed to load). **Edit 2** The author was convinced with this feature being useful. [He is planning](https://github.com/verlok/lazyload/issues/324#issuecomment-472196151) to add the revived image lazy loading feature on a future release. I thought it might help figuring out if this is worth including this in the algorithm as well.

My understanding is that current language is sufficient, as it calls "selecting an image source", which is taking picture processing into account. With that said, it's not clear when the "image metadata fetching" algorithm runs, which [may result in the wrong resource fetched](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/3752/files#r263757315) if it runs before the element is actually added to its `<picture>` parent. Hey @zcorpan :) 

I've taken a quick look at the [related definitions](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/media.html#attr-video-poster) for `poster`, and the logic there seems quite disconnected from the overall logic for [image loading](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#update-the-image-data). Given that we're planning to add different logic to an attribute with a different name, I don't see any urgency in doing all that distinct work as part of a single PR.

As you point out, a `loadpolicy` attribute can make sense for the video content itself as well as its poster, so IMO both can be tackled together, and separately from this PR. Does that make sense?

Hey guys, Have anyone considered how does `loading="lazy"` affect responsive images and `srcset` and `sizes` attributes? When user agent parses HTML, it has no idea what's `` size in the page is gonna be. To load it as quickly as possible (before layout is done and even before any CSS is downloaded) we need to provide `sizes` attribute to hint browser how large is image gonna be: `` Unfortunately, `sizes` attribute is frequently forgotten by developers making websites load too large images (`sizes` defaults to `100vw`). However, **`sizes` attribute is extremely redundant in most cases!**. If image can be loaded **after** layout phase (most below-the-fold images can), the browser already knows its size so it could pick best image based on `srcset` only **without** `sizes` at all. Instead, browsers automatically pick the best version of image from `srcset`. I believe it would reduce a huge amount of mistakes being caused by lack of `sizes` attribute (which is de facto duplication of CSS logic, because CSS already says how big image will be). The most ridiculous situation (and common one) is when image sits in a grid (let's say 4 items in a row, so it's 350px wide in 1920px browser), is below-the-fold, it's loaded 10 seconds after page is loaded, it is obvious at this point in time it's 350px wide. Alt text is displayed as visible content when images _fail_ to load, or when users have _disabled_ image loading.  But when image loading is active, I believe most user agents currently wait until they've tried to load an image before displaying the `alt`.

My personal opinion: if the lazy loaded image will be fetched automatically when it comes into view, it's reasonable to delay display of the `alt` text until the fetch has timed out or returned an error. But if the image won't be fully fetched unless triggered by the user, it may be helpful to display the `alt` text to help the user decide if the image will be worth the data charges.
